title: GPU time in the Experiment 8 logs: 25 of 82 Qwen generation passes died while starting vLLM
body:
Thanks for releasing the full tool logs, they made this easy to check.

I went through the `tool_calls.jsonl` of the 7 Experiment 8 sessions (logs at `4d09ba6d`) to see where the GPU time goes. A few numbers that might help with the harness:

- 25 of the 82 Qwen generation passes died while starting a vLLM engine. Those failed attempts are 16 to 27% of each Qwen session's GPU time.
- 95% of generation passes are paired (same problems through the original and the edited model). Since the base model never changes within a session, 19 to 40% of all generated tokens re-sample it on problems it already answered in an earlier pass (estimated from each half's reported mean length). Reusing those earlier base samples would remove them.
- In the released MATH-500 outputs, about 70% of the base model's tokens come after it starts repeating itself.
- Passes are bound by decode steps more than by batch size: at 32,768 tokens, passes with 128 answers took a median of 986 s, with 256 answers 950 s, and with 512 answers 1,316 s. So passes from different sessions could share a batch.

I also checked that p50c served as a rank-1 LoRA adapter in vLLM (ie. in the same batch as the base model) keeps its gain: 44/64 vs 10/64 for the base model on 64 practice problems at 32,768 tokens.

Scripts and numbers: https://github.com/fus3r/wspserve (`experiments/workload.py`, `results/workload.json`). Write-up: https://fus3r.github.io/blog/wsp-session-cost/

Happy to share more detail if any of this is useful.

title: Fix acc_lenient always null for non-sharded eval runs in merge.py
body:
## Summary

`evaluate.py` always writes `ok_lenient` into `scores.json` (`exp8_math/code/evaluate.py:188`). `merge.py` aggregates it correctly for sharded runs (the `parts/*/scores.json` loop), but the non-sharded "full" `scores.json` branch never reads `ok_lenient` at all. Since `acc_lenient` in `merged.json` is only computed `if a.get("ok_lenient") is not None`, any non-sharded eval run silently gets `acc_lenient: null`, even though the value needed to compute it is sitting right there in `scores.json`.

One-line fix: carry `ok_lenient` through in the full-scores branch the same way the other fields already do (`v.get(...)`).

## Test plan

Verified with a standalone script against a synthetic non-sharded `scores.json` (`ok_lenient: 1650`, `total: 2000`):
- Before the fix: `acc_lenient` → `None`
- After the fix: `acc_lenient` → `0.825` (matches `1650 / 2000`)

Sharded aggregation behavior is untouched.

title: Record the induction cutoff alongside exp3 true_copy_heads
body:
In the released `exp3_language/eval/scores.json`, `true_copy_heads` uses a cutoff of 0.3, while the post and the README table use 0.2. The [README already explains this](https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/blob/4d09ba6d6a7e891dd8063974dfe81b3d78e3494f/exp3_language/README.md), but the JSON records don't identify their cutoff, so a reader using the scores alone gets a different comparison.

At commit `4d09ba6d6a7e891dd8063974dfe81b3d78e3494f`, the Python heads above 0.2 are `L2H1`, `L3H1`, and `L3H5`; the stored truth contains only `L3H5`. Romaji has `L3H3` above 0.2 but an empty stored truth list. English has `L3H1` under both cutoffs. These can be checked from the repository root without loading a model:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("exp3_language/eval")
heads = json.loads((root / "heads.json").read_text())
scores = json.loads((root / "scores.json").read_text())
for row in scores:
    measured = heads[row["net"]]
    print(row["id"], {
        "above_0.2": [h for h, v in measured.items() if v["induct"] > 0.2],
        "above_0.3": [h for h, v in measured.items() if v["induct"] > 0.3],
        "stored": row["true_copy_heads"],
    })
```

Could you add explicit cutoff metadata or a separate derived score file for the post's 0.2 definition? Keeping the original score files intact would preserve the experimental record while making the intended comparison easier to reproduce.

title: Independent peer-audit follow-up: five open questions after #4, #5, and the HF third-party replication
body:
Hi — first, thank you for releasing the checkpoints, the bit-exact diff, the full logs, and the graded outputs. This post is only possible because you did.

I come from an independent multi-perspective audit of the blog post (structured like #4 and #5, but run separately). Where #4 (carlostoledo1891) and the Hugging Face rebuild by ML-Intern-lab have already settled questions, I simply confirm and link. My goal here is the five things that I believe nobody has raised yet — in the spirit of making the record stronger, not dimming it.

## What I verified and endorse (no new asks)

- The edit arithmetic is exact: 131,072 = 2×64×1024 (down_proj, layers 15 & 19), 131,072/800M ≈ 0.016% — all recompute.
- The HF third-party rebuild ([ML-Intern-lab/Qwen3.5-0.8B-weight-space-programming](https://huggingface.co/ML-Intern-lab/Qwen3.5-0.8B-weight-space-programming)) is a serious replication: bit-exact diff re-applied with sha256 tensor verification, full 500-problem × 4-sample MATH-500 re-eval with the paper's protocol, raw score files published. Edited score 51.0% vs the paper's 48.1%, token-limit 31.6% vs 33.1%.
- #4's pre-registered baseline re-run (untouched model at Qwen's recommended non-thinking settings scores 44–52%) and its finding that `experiment_history` computes W = W₀ − 6·outer(u, mask·(uᵀW₀)) — reverse-and-amplify, not "subtracted" — are, in my reading, accurate and the most important external checks so far.
- Sol Messing's independent thread ([@SolomonMg, Nov 3](https://x.com/SolomonMg/status/2117650796342894884)) adds a point nobody else made: the edit is far more consequential in *mass* than "3.5% of weights" suggests — the largest edited weight goes from ~0.095 to ~876. Whether the intended frame is count-sparsity or magnitude-sparsity deserves one clarifying sentence.

## Five open questions (not yet raised in #1–#7, as far as I can tell)

### 1. Non-monotonic effects of the pass count — one direction, or several?

From 10 → 25 passes, GSM8K *drops* 25.7 → 25.1 and IFEval *drops* 49.0 → 39.9, before jumping at 50 passes. If the mechanism is "remove one loop direction," I'd expect monotonic (or at least non-degrading) behavior in pass count. Related: 33.1% of edited-model MATH-500 answers (31.6% in the HF re-eval) still hit the token limit. Is the loop pathology one direction with clean removal, or a mixture where the edit removes only the dominant component? The released logs likely already contain the data to answer this.

### 2. Experiment 6's headline comparison has no numbers

Exp 6 claims beating "an equal-sized PPO trained on 20M games" (1.48M params), but the scoring section specifies only two *small* opponents (~16k params), and no win rate, margin, or Elo-style figure appears anywhere. Could you publish the opponent spec, protocol, and the actual win rate behind that sentence?

### 3. Multi-seed variance for the headline edit results

The PPO baselines are reported as best-of-3–10 seeds, while the Astra edit results (Exp 8: 7.9 → 48.1; Exp 5) are single seed-0 runs. The 48.1% (paper) vs 51.0% (HF re-eval, same seed and protocol) gap already hints at nontrivial sensitivity to stack/hardware details. Would you publish ≥5 independent edit sessions per headline result (mean ± sd, per-session success histogram)? If 48.1 is a best-of-N draw rather than a mean, the core claim changes materially — I'd rather know it's robust.

### 4. Closing the loop on #4 and the framing numbers

Two small closures that would make the record airtight:

- (a) Confirm or correct the "subtracted that direction" wording against the actual reverse-and-amplify update (#4), and clarify the 884 bf16 entries that differ but round back.
- (b) One sentence on the count-vs-mass framing of "0.016%" / "3.5% of weights" (Messing's point above): the *number* of edited weights is tiny; their *magnitude* is not.

Neither changes the result — both change how a reader calibrates it.

### 5. The "no search" boundary in Exp 3

Qwen's repetition/loop pathology is pre-documented in its own model card, and the Exp 3 localization procedure closely matches published induction-head ablation methodology (Elhage et al.). So "Astra found it by reading weights, without any search" is hard to separate from "Astra recalled public literature about this exact model and method class." A cheap control would sharpen the claim: one pathology with **no** public literature (or a custom architecture), reported with the same rigor as Exp 8. Until then, I'd suggest softening the Exp 3 framing from "discovered" to "recovered."

## Closing

None of the above dims the core result. Exp 8, now with two independent external replications (#4's byte-level re-derivation and the HF rebuild), is real and striking — and the paper's honest negatives (Gemma unimprovable; weights-only auditing failing 4/4) are its best feature. These five asks are about causal *strength*, *precision* of claims, and variance reporting — the things that turn a striking result into a durable one.

Happy to share the full audit write-up if useful.

title: Experiment 2 diffusion events.jsonl
body:
Hi,

Like many, I was quite impressed with the potential of your work to open a new direction in optimization where instead of backpropagation to optimize networks behavior, LLMs directly reason about weights and employ their knowledge to tune values.

While looking at experiment 2 events.jsonl, for example: exp2_diffusion/runs/square/events.jsonl , i noticed the first turn says:

`{"type":"turn.started"}
{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"item_1","type":"reasoning","text":"**Analyzing rectangle geometry**\n**Comparing rectangle edge patterns**\n**Checking row indexing**"}}`

And similarly for circle and triangle, they seem begin by checking for the shape they want to find.
Also in the triangle case:

`Narrow edge patterns favor hollow triangles over filled ones. Rectangles lack these sloping sides; circles lack the straight base and converging edges. An “A” is less consistent with the horizontal strokes being concentrated toward the bottom rather than forming a middle crossbar.`

As I couldn’t find a mention of shapes in the prompt, I was wondering why the model seems to begin with the assumption that it is looking for, say, a rectangle and then, a few turns later, finds one. 

Did I misunderstood the setup or the events.jsonl format ?

In any case, this is a very exciting research direction and I don’t doubt that the concept of weight space programming will offer new ways to fix unwanted behaviors or vastly imrpovr initialization, which I believe are two areas classical techniques often struggle with.

title: The Role of Human Priors in Weight-Space Programming (Exp. 7 & 8)
body:
Congratulations on this fascinating work! I really enjoyed reading the blog and exploring the released experimental logs. The results are impressive, especially the ability to directly inspect and modify neural network weights without gradient-based training. Thank you for making the experimental traces publicly available!

I have a few questions about the role of human-provided priors in these experiments.

1. How important was the human-provided failure hypothesis in Experiment 8?

I noticed that the prompt explicitly mentions repetition and failure to finish as potential failure modes. Astra eventually identified and repaired a looping-related mechanism, leading to a substantial improvement in mathematical performance.

I'm curious how much this prior guidance contributed to the success. Have you tried a more open-ended prompt that simply asks Astra to improve mathematical performance, without explicitly suggesting possible failure modes or diagnostic strategies?

Such a prompt ablation could help distinguish between Astra's ability to autonomously discover failure mechanisms and its ability to investigate and repair mechanisms suggested by humans.

2. Could similar human priors improve the unsuccessful experiments?

For example, in Experiment 7 (sycophancy detection), Astra struggled to distinguish the models using weights alone.

I wonder whether providing more targeted human priors about potential mechanisms or relevant weight-space structures could improve its performance, similar to the guidance provided in Experiment 8.

This could also reveal an interesting trade-off between the amount of human guidance and the agent's ability to successfully analyze neural networks.

3. More experiments and failure cases

I'd also love to see more experiments, especially unsuccessful attempts and their corresponding traces. Understanding when and why Astra fails could be just as informative as the successful examples, and could help clarify the current limitations of autonomous weight-space reasoning.

Overall, I find this research direction very exciting and look forward to seeing how it develops. Thanks again for the excellent work and for sharing the logs!

title: Independent re-run of the MATH-500 baseline under Qwen's recommended settings: the untouched model scores 44–52%
body:
Hi — thank you for releasing the checkpoint, the bit-exact diff, the logs and the graded outputs; this is only possible because you did.

I decided the edit from the bytes (two implementations sharing no code) and re-graded every released MATH-500 answer with an exact three-valued grader: the edit is exactly as released (two tensors, sha256 as your card prints), and my grading agrees with math-verify on every decided first-sample answer. Two small things: 130,188 bf16 entries differ (131,072 are addressed; 884 round back), and the formula in your experiment_history is W = W₀ − 6·outer(u, mask·(uᵀW₀)), so the loop component is reversed and amplified, not subtracted — the post's text says "subtracted".

Then the baseline, pre-registered before the run (notes/wsp-stage3-preregistration-2026-11-02.md), vLLM 0.33.0, your prompt and chat template, 4 samples × 500, seed 0:

| arm | setting | first sample (floor / decided) | all 2,000 (floor / decided) | answered | hit the limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | your settings (temp 0.6, thinking, 32,768) | 7.8% / 7.8% | 7.2% / 7.2% | 8% | 93.1% |
| C3 | Qwen card, non-thinking text (temp 1.0, top_p 1.0, presence 2.0, 32,768) | 45.6% / 51.7% | 44.0% / 49.8% | 98.5% | 0.3% |

("floor" counts an answer my grader refuses as wrong; "decided" is CORRECT over CORRECT + WRONG.) C2 (the card's thinking settings, 81,920 tokens) and C4 (your edited checkpoint under C2) are running and will be added to the same record.

So under the model card's own recommended settings the unedited model lands where the edited one lands under yours. The edit is real and it does what your logs say — it stops the loop — but the "6×" is measured against a looping regime the card itself warns about. I'd read the result as "the edit recovers what the recommended settings give", and I'd be glad to be shown a setting where that is not so.

From your logs I also checked the claims going around: the dose (6) was chosen over 3,680 practice answers (GSM8K/MATH train), never a MATH-500 problem by id or text; the Frogger/Freeway keyword rule is as your README states; the car policy's edited weights reach 876 and the 100% is 1,280 episodes on one level; the sycophancy round failed from the weights alone in your own words. Record: certs/wsp-side-claims.json.

Everything is pinned (sha256 of every input), every verdict is in the records, and the grader is 300 lines of standard-library Python you can read: https://carlostoledo.co/reports/weight-space-programming.html — records at https://github.com/carlostoledo1891/cert-machine/tree/main/certs (wsp-weights.json, wsp-regrade.json, wsp-baseline.json, wsp-side-claims.json).

I'll hold the public summary for 24 h from this issue so you can point out anything I misread. — Carlos

title: Add Experiment 5 scorer: read a reply into a network and score it on MinAtar
body:
The release has the Experiment 5 replies, networks and scores, but no code to read a reply into a network or to score a network. This adds `exp5_write_from_scratch/code/score.py` and a short section in that folder's README.

**What it does**
- Reads a reply the way the prompt describes: only the last `edits` block, statements in order, a statement that cannot be read is skipped. It accepts the `[ [ ... ] ]` form mentioned in the README.
- Scores a network with the protocol in the prompt: MinAtar 1.0.15, sticky actions 0.1, actions sampled from the softmax, at most 10,000 steps, 1,000 episodes. It prints the same fields as `eval/minatar_eval.json`.
- `--save` writes the network read from a reply in the `hand.npz` format.

**Checks**
- Reading `runs/<game>/reply/answer.md` gives `networks/<game>/hand.npz` exactly (float32-identical), with the same statement counts as `apply.json` (92 / 122 / 55, 0 errors).
- Scoring the released networks (seed 0):

| Game | `eval/minatar_eval.json` | `code/score.py` |
|---|---|---|
| Breakout | 517.4 ± 7.4 | 502.8 ± 7.7 |
| Seaquest | 53.1 ± 1.4 | 52.6 ± 1.4 |
| Asterix | 53.2 ± 1.0 | 52.4 ± 1.0 |

The differences are within episode noise (different random streams for the game and the action sampling). If your scorer did anything differently, for example resetting `last_action` between episodes or a different seeding scheme, I'm happy to match it.
